subject: 52B1C3F2B9574C37BAF0ECCC8D5AB8C1
introduction: How is the soul related to the body? The guide refuses the easiest picture, of a vessel and what it holds, and offers others in its place: the sun and the mirror, the user and the instrument, the bird and the cage, the meaning and the word. Its ninety quotations are read here with ninety from elsewhere. Scripture speaks of dust and breath, of a treasure in earthen vessels, of an outward man that perishes while the inward is renewed; Plato, the Upanishads and the Gita speak of a prisoner, a rider in a chariot, a wearer of robes. Against them stand those who will not let the two be parted. Aristotle thinks the question as idle as asking whether wax and its shape are one; Simmias fears the soul is only the tuning of the lyre; Hume cannot find the self that says ‘I’; Whitman asks what the soul is if not the body; and Marvell lets the body complain of the soul. Paul stands on both sides, longing to depart and choosing to remain, calling the body a temple and keeping it under. The contrasts are placed where the guide’s own images are being tested.
questions: The guide prefers the sun and the mirror to the cup and the water. What does the first image explain that the second cannot?
Aristotle and Simmias both suggest that the soul cannot be separated from the body. Which of the guide's arguments answers them most directly, and how well?
Several readings say that illness and old age do not touch the soul, while Proverbs says a merry heart is medicine and envy rots the bones. How do the two directions of influence fit together?
The body is called a cage, an instrument, a temple and a word. What way of treating one's own body follows from each?
Marvell lets the body complain of the soul. What would a fair reply be?
Paul wishes to depart and decides to stay because it is more needful for others. What does his choice suggest about what bodily life is for?

outside.why: Paul uses the mirror as well: beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, we are changed into the same image.
Plotinus uses the sun for a source that gives without being altered: a brilliant light ceaselessly generated from an unchanging substance.
Hume, entering most intimately into what he calls himself, always stumbles on some particular perception and never catches himself without one. What answers his report?
The Katha Upanishad separates the rider from the vehicle: the Self sits in the chariot, and the body is the chariot.
Paul cannot tell whether the man he knew was in the body or out of the body: God knows. Is 'in' or 'out' the right question to ask about the spirit at all?

Aristotle dismisses the question whether soul and body are one, as he would the question whether the wax and the shape stamped on it are one. If the soul is the body's form, can it be without the body?
Paul speaks of a treasure held in earthen vessels. Does his image say the same as the cup and the water that the guide sets aside, or something else?
Marcus Aurelius repeats a saying of Epictetus: thou art a little soul bearing about a corpse. What is wrong, on the guide's account, with that picture of the body?
Paul writes to friends of being absent in the flesh and yet with them in the spirit.
The Qur'an answers questions about the Spirit by saying it is by command of the Lord, and that little knowledge has been given.
Proverbs calls the spirit of man the candle of the Lord, searching all the inward parts.
Jesus speaks of light and the body together: the light of the body is the eye, and it is to be single.
The Qur'an's similitude of light sets a lamp in a niche, the lamp in a glass, and the glass like a shining star.
Shelley pictures life as a dome of many-coloured glass which stains the white radiance of eternity.
The Qur'an says that God receives souls at death and, for those not yet dying, in their sleep, and dismisses these until an appointed term.
Prospero says the actors were all spirits and are melted into thin air, like the baseless fabric of a vision. Do dreams show the soul's freedom from the body, or the frailty of all we perceive?
Dickinson finds the brain wider than the sky, since it will contain the sky with ease, and you beside.
Hamlet's praise runs through the powers: how noble in reason, how infinite in faculty, in apprehension how like a god.
Simmias objects that harmony is invisible, incorporeal and divine and yet abides in a lyre made of matter. If the mind is the tuning of the body, what becomes of it when the strings break?
Aristotle holds that reason, more than anything else, is man, and that the life according to reason is best.
Elihu says in Job that there is a spirit in man, and that the inspiration of the Almighty gives understanding.
Paul's image for a living whole is the body, which is one and has many members.
Paul notes that the many members of one body do not all have the same office.
The psalmist praises God for being fearfully and wonderfully made, and adds that his soul knows it right well.
Jesus compares the spirit to the wind, which blows where it lists and is known by its sound.
Paul was told that strength is made perfect in weakness, and so would rather glory in his infirmities.
James takes it as the plainest of comparisons: the body without the spirit is dead.
Job recalls being fashioned round about by God's hands and made as the clay.
Plato's Timaeus watches the elements pass into one another, water becoming stone and earth by condensation.
Isaiah's image for the composed body is clay and potter: we are all the work of thy hand.
Genesis tells of two moments: the forming of man from the dust of the ground, and the breath of life by which he became a living soul.
In the Qur'an God first makes the human being and then breathes into him of his Spirit.
Zechariah names God as the one who stretches out the heavens and forms the spirit of man within him.
Whitman asks: if the body were not the soul, what is the soul? Is that a denial of the spirit, or a refusal to despise the body?
Paul's seed is sown as bare grain and is given a body afterwards, to every seed its own body.
Jesus says that a corn of wheat abides alone unless it falls into the ground and dies, and then brings forth much fruit.
In Jesus's parable the seed springs and grows, the sower knows not how: first the blade, then the ear.
Plato's Socrates holds that the soul is immortal and has been born again many times. What follows for a life if the soul's individuality begins with the body instead?
Wordsworth imagines the soul coming from afar, not in entire forgetfulness. What draws people to the thought of a life before this one?
Jeremiah hears: before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee. Does being known beforehand require having existed beforehand?
The Qur'an follows the body through its stages, clot and little lump and bones and flesh, and then speaks of another creation.
Samuel is told that man looks on the outward appearance, but the Lord looks on the heart.
The Preacher says that man and beast have one breath and that a man has no preeminence above a beast. What must be added to his observation for the guide's claim to stand?
Pascal seeks human dignity not from space but from thought, by which he comprehends the world.
Jesus notes that John came neither eating nor drinking, while the Son of man came eating and drinking, and both were blamed.
Proverbs runs the connection from within outward: a sound heart is the life of the flesh, and envy the rottenness of the bones.
Proverbs has the merry heart doing good like a medicine, and the broken spirit drying the bones.
In Proverbs pleasant words are sweet to the soul and health to the bones in the same breath.
The elder's wish for his friend joins the two: that he may be in health, even as his soul prospers.
Paul says that though the outward man perish, the inward man is renewed day by day.
Jesus says that the spirit indeed is willing but the flesh is weak. When does a weak body leave the spirit free, and when does it drag it down?
Proverbs says the spirit of a man will sustain his infirmity, and asks who can bear a wounded spirit.
Paul rejects the ascetic's refusals: every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be refused.
Paul asks why those who are dead with Christ should be subject to ordinances such as 'touch not, taste not, handle not'.
Paul keeps under his body and brings it into subjection, like one who strives for the mastery. Where is the line between discipline of the body and contempt for it?
Paul calls the body the temple of the Holy Ghost. Is a temple more than an instrument, and does that change how the body should be treated?
Marvell lets the body answer back: the soul warms and moves a needless frame, and has made it live to let it die. What would the guide say to the body's complaint?
Paul names the three together in a prayer for his friends: your whole spirit and soul and body.
Hebrews speaks of a word sharp enough to divide soul and spirit, as it divides the joints and marrow.
Plato's Socrates concludes that the soul is in the likeness of the divine and immortal, and the body in the likeness of the human and mortal.
Lovelace says that stone walls do not a prison make, nor iron bars a cage, for minds innocent and quiet.
Epictetus holds that men are disturbed not by things but by the principles and notions which they form concerning things.
The psalmist admits that his flesh and his heart fail, and names God as the strength of his heart.
Lorenzo says there is harmony in immortal souls which we cannot hear while this muddy vesture of decay closes it in.
Yeats calls an aged man a tattered coat upon a stick, unless soul clap its hands and sing. Is the soul's singing a fact about old age, or a task set for it?
Jesus tells his followers not to fear those who kill the body but are not able to kill the soul.
Paul expects that if the earthly house of this tabernacle were dissolved, there is a house not made with hands.
The Preacher's ending sends the dust back to the earth as it was, and the spirit to God who gave it.
Job declares that his redeemer lives and that in his flesh he shall see God. Why might a tradition hold on to the body even in its hope beyond death?
The Gita says that the spirit was never born and shall never cease to be.
Paul is in a strait between departing and abiding in the flesh, and judges that to abide is more needful for others. If the body is unimportant, why is remaining in it a service?
Jesus asks whether the life is not more than meat, and the body more than raiment.
The Dhammapada foresees this body lying on the earth, despised and without understanding, like a useless log.
Hamlet follows imperious Caesar's body, dead and turned to clay, to where it might stop a hole to keep the wind away.
Genesis says of the body that it was taken out of the ground: dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return.
Paul's sequence is the same: it is sown a natural body, and it is raised a spiritual body.
Paul says that while we are at home in the body we walk by faith, not by sight, and would rather be absent from it.
The phrase comes from Genesis, where God says: let us make man in our image, after our likeness.
Ezekiel hears God claim every soul as his own: behold, all souls are mine, the father's and the son's alike.
The psalm has the same picture of release: our soul is escaped as a bird out of the snare of the fowlers.
The psalmist longs for wings like a dove, so that he might fly away and be at rest.
In the Phaedo the soul is able to view existence only through the bars of a prison, and not in her own nature.
Marvell's soul describes its cage part by part: bolts of bones, fettered in feet, manacled in hands, blinded with an eye.
Paul cries out to be delivered from the body of this death, having found another law warring in his members. Is the body itself the cage, or something that has happened in it?
Paul's contrast of letter and spirit has the same shape: the letter kills, but the spirit gives life.
John says that the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us. What does it say about bodies that a meaning should need a word in order to be beheld?
Juvenal's counsel is to leave to the gods what is good for us, and to pray for a sound mind in a sound body.
The Gita pictures the spirit putting by its garb of flesh as one lays worn-out robes away and takes new ones.
Paul, citing poets his hearers knew, says that in God we live, and move, and have our being.
Lucretius argues from the nothing before birth to the nothing after death. What in the guide's account of the soul would he first have to be shown?

philippians-to-depart-or-to-abide.text: For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain. But if I live in the flesh, this is the fruit of my labour: yet what I shall choose I wot not. For I am in a strait betwixt two, having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better: Nevertheless to abide in the flesh is more needful for you

james-body-without-the-spirit.text: For as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead also

matthew-life-more-than-meat.text: Therefore I say unto you, Take no thought for your life, what ye shall eat, or what ye shall drink; nor yet for your body, what ye shall put on. Is not the life more than meat, and the body than raiment

job-in-my-flesh-shall-i-see-god.text: For I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth: And though after my skin worms destroy this body, yet in my flesh shall I see God: Whom I shall see for myself, and mine eyes shall behold, and not another; though my reins be consumed within me

job-clothed-me-with-skin-and-flesh.text: Thine hands have made me and fashioned me together round about; yet thou dost destroy me. Remember, I beseech thee, that thou hast made me as the clay; and wilt thou bring me into dust again? Hast thou not poured me out as milk, and curdled me like cheese? Thou hast clothed me with skin and flesh, and hast fenced me with bones and sinews. Thou hast granted me life and favour, and thy visitation hath preserved my spirit

psalm-wings-like-a-dove.text: And I said, Oh that I had wings like a dove! for then would I fly away, and be at rest

colossians-neglecting-of-the-body.text: Wherefore if ye be dead with Christ from the rudiments of the world, why, as though living in the world, are ye subject to ordinances, (Touch not; taste not; handle not; Which all are to perish with the using;) after the commandments and doctrines of men? Which things have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body: not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh

matthew-came-eating-and-drinking.text: For John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, He hath a devil. The Son of man came eating and drinking, and they say, Behold a man gluttonous, and a winebibber, a friend of publicans and sinners. But wisdom is justified of her children

proverbs-sound-heart-life-of-the-flesh.text: A sound heart is the life of the flesh: but envy the rottenness of the bones

proverbs-pleasant-words-health-to-the-bo.text: Pleasant words are as an honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones

isaiah-we-are-the-clay.text: But now, O Lord, thou art our father; we are the clay, and thou our potter; and we all are the work of thy hand

psalm-flesh-and-heart-faileth.text: My flesh and my heart faileth: but God is the strength of my heart, and my portion for ever

dhammapada-useless-log.text: Before long, alas! this body will lie on the earth, despised, without understanding, like a useless log

aristotle-wax-and-its-shape.text: That is why we can wholly dismiss as unnecessary the question whether the soul and the body are one: it is as meaningless as to ask whether the wax and the shape given to it by the stamp are one
aristotle-wax-and-its-shape.author: Aristotle

marvell-bolts-of-bones.text: With bolts of Bones, that fetter'd stands / In Feet; and manacled in Hands. / Here blinded with an Eye; and there / Deaf with the drumming of an Ear
marvell-bolts-of-bones.author: Andrew Marvell
marvell-bolts-of-bones.work: A Dialogue between the Soul and Body

marvell-this-tyrannic-soul.text: O who shall me deliver whole, / From bonds of this Tyrannic Soul? / Which, stretcht upright, impales me so, / That mine own Precipice I go; / And warms and moves this needless Frame: / (A Fever could but do the same.) / And, wanting where its spight to try, / Has made me live to let me dye
marvell-this-tyrannic-soul.author: Andrew Marvell
marvell-this-tyrannic-soul.work: A Dialogue between the Soul and Body

whitman-if-the-body-were-not-the-soul.text: And if the body does not do fully as much as the soul? / And if the body were not the soul, what is the soul?
whitman-if-the-body-were-not-the-soul.author: Walt Whitman

yeats-soul-clap-its-hands.text: An aged man is but a paltry thing, / A tattered coat upon a stick, unless / Soul clap its hands and sing, and louder sing / For every tatter in its mortal dress
yeats-soul-clap-its-hands.author: W. B. Yeats

plato-harmony-and-the-lyre.text: Might not a person use the same argument about harmony and the lyre-might he not say that harmony is a thing invisible, incorporeal, fair, divine, abiding in the lyre which is harmonized, but that the lyre and the strings are matter and material, composite, earthy, and akin to mortality
plato-harmony-and-the-lyre.author: Plato
